blocks.p: Music is the next safety anchoring potential. Of course, music comes in through our sense of hearing. But it deserves its own lesson since there is so much to it.

Music might be one of your most immediately impactful safety cues. Clients often use music as a means to feel generally better. And sometimes they use music to simply feel anything at all. My adolescent and teen clients deeply resonate with music and experience it as a piece of who they are.

However, I don't think they initially know why it helps or how to make the most use of it. But they know it does something for them that feels generally good. Music is easily accessible and potentially a fantastic means to anchor in safety. Let's make sure we're utilizing it as efficiently as possible.

Music is global, from Brazilian samba to South Asian qawwali to taiko drumming from Japan. Though global and infinitely diverse, music speaks to each of us on a deep and personal level. It understands us. It soothes us. It plays with us. And it energizes us. So much so that music can somehow compel our bodies to move without conscious awareness. Even I, who hates dancing, will spontaneously join in a passive rhythm without realizing it. My foot will tap, or my head will start nodding along. And I even have my moments of singing in the car or with my kids.
Music can act as a safety cue or anchor.

Music can be on in the background, passively cueing safety as one works on another task. In fact, I am listening to Apple Music's Creative Focus playlist as I write this. Well, I say I'm "listening," but really, I'm not. Music is on, but I'm not paying attention to it. My focus is on thinking and writing. The music provides me with a passive cue of safety, aiding me in my goal of writing. If music were an active safety cue for me, I could stop writing and dance spontaneously. (But we both know that's not happening.)

But music is also an active safety anchor. I could stop writing, close my eyes, and listen to the music. Then, I could notice how each little note triggers my system. I'd notice the deep basses trigger a slight sensation in my gut. And the more melodic sounds create a fluttery playfulness in my chest. I could welcome the experience and practice a few extended exhales as I listen. And if I mindfully attuned to my inner world with enough curiosity and compassion: who knows? My body may start moving around along with the music (I believe this is dancing).

Vocal prosody uses a fuller voice range with a sing-songy quality. When you hear someone using vocal prosody, it provides a safety cue to your system. Prosody is a passive safety cue, something you don't need to do anything about consciously. When a parent soothes their baby through prosody, the baby does not need to think about the parent's voice. The prosodic voice simply provides co-regulative soothing. Same with the melodic voice we use with our pets, which causes them to come closer to us.

Not only do you have a fuller range of voice when in safety, but you're capable of purposefully using your voice to indicate intention. You can use the same words to show different feelings or intentions. For example, when asking a question, there may be a higher pitch at the end of the sentence to indicate curiosity. Say these sentences out loud and listen for a difference in your voice -

On the other hand, a lack of vocal prosody is a danger cue. When one does not have vocal prosody, their voice will be more high-pitched with anxiety, low-pitched with anger, or low and dull without energy (think Ben Stein). They have lost the fuller range of voice between those extremes. The lack of vocal prosody triggers the listener's neuroception of mild danger, possibly enough to experience boredom, fear, or an impulse to get away or be aggressive. When you talk to your dog with a stern, flat voice, they react in shame and pull away (even if you're using kind words).

When we hear someone using vocal prosody, it indicates they have access to their safety state, making them a safe mammal. In the presence of a safe mammal and a safe environment, individuals in a dysregulated state can receive co-regulation, which involves receiving safety cues from a safe other. This co-regulation helps us climb our Polyvagal ladder.

We can also receive these co-regulatory vocal prosody safety cues by listening to music incorporating vocal prosody. Dr. Porges developed the Safe and Sound Protocol, which is music specifically designed to enhance prosody to support regulation, originally intended for those on the autism spectrum. The protocol has elicited spontaneous social behaviors when combined with a supportive person in the room. Professionals have applied this approach to various populations. You can see the ingredients for regulation: safe person, safe place, and prosodic music.
Although our favorite singer may not be in the room with us, their singing indicates their access to safety. We can still pick up on the safety cues they express through their singing.

But not all music contains vocal prosody. Some genres, like rap and heavy metal, may have more monotone or aggressive sounds that lack vocal range. Pantera and TuPac contrast with singers like Etta James or the Beach Boys.

Aside from the vocal prosody in a song, there is also musical prosody. The instruments themselves send our system notes of safety or danger. When notes combine, they bring us joy, play, excitement, and more. The heavy bass of rap music probably brings someone to a more aggressive mobilization. The range of a classical symphony can bring us up and down our Polyvagal ladder.

Like the other safety anchors, focus primarily on how music affects your feelings of safety. That's the priority. But it's also important to understand that music affects us based on our state. Music Type A will affect your shutdown state in a way that feels right, while Music Type B feels wrong. But Type B might feel right when you're in a fight state. Luckily, finding music that aligns with your state is fairly easy. In fact, you're probably already listening to music that aligns with your state!

Certain songs or genres align with your current Polyvagal state. They simply feel right to your system. These pieces of music understand you on a deep level, echoing into your body and your nervous system needs in the present moment. Think back to when you were an angsty teen: was there a song you kept on repeat? Do you currently have a go-to song for breakups and feeling alone? Is there a song you turn to when you need to cry or when you're ready to party? How about before or during a workout? These are all music you connect with from your current dominant state.

Finding music that aligns with your current state becomes a pathway for introspection, allowing you to explore your inner world. It grants permission for your biology to be in its state without rejection. The music rolls out the red carpet for your conscious mind to connect with your bottom-up experiences.

State Alignment Music can also potentially help prevent dysregulation when you're in defense. It can help you feel understood and connected, providing validation and normalization. It can also help you give permission for defensive activation to be present.

Conversely, State Alignment Music could reinforce your defensive activation and potentially worsen it. For example, when you feel alone and turn to your go-to lonely song on repeat, does it help you come out of a lonely shutdown? Or, does it potentially reinforce it? And with the state reinforcement come thoughts that you'll be alone forever and nothing will get better.

If you're pulled toward State Alignment Music, keep in mind you may be on a teeter totter: the music can help contain defense or deepen it. There is nothing wrong with State Alignment Music and it can be beneficial by containing or even permitting defense, though this is most beneficial when you are anchored in safety and can mindfully listen.
Music doesn't just passively connect with your current state. It can actually help assist self-regulation if you listen mindfully. There are two pathways to activating safety through music.

When you listen mindfully to music aligned with your current state, you may eventually notice you're ready for another type. The next type of music could bolster and encourage self-regulation. This type of music may be one rung above your current state, offering gentle assistance toward a higher level of regulation and safety.

For example, when in a shutdown state, aggressive and loud heavy metal doesn't align and will likely provide a neuroception of danger, reinforcing the shutdown. However, melancholic music can provide an avenue to mindfully connect with the inner experience of shutdown. The mindful connection allows self-regulation from shutdown to unfold. As shutdown alleviates and mobility fills the system, the previously avoided aggressive and loud heavy metal music may draw out the emerging flight/fight activation, encouraging further self-regulation. The body is now ready for mobilization, so faster and louder music is more appealing.

This option is great for intentionally self-regulating out of a stuck defensive state. You can mindfully listen to music that aligns with your state, then shift music based on the needs of your body in the present moment. This can take you from shutdown to fight, from fight to flight, then flight to safety. This takes a high level of mindfulness of your inner experiences based on the external music. This is especially powerful when combined with movement.

Another option is to listen to music that provides a neuroception of safety and triggers your safety pathways. Music that triggers safety doesn't necessarily align with or connect with your stuck defensive state. It just triggers safety. Similarly, people tell me my voice feels safe for them on the podcast or a recorded meditation inside of the [Unstucking Academy](https://www.stucknotbroken.com/checkout/co-regulator). My voice doesn't align with their defensive state; it just connects to their safety state.

Safety Cueing Music Option 2 music can trigger safety, seemingly bypassing defense. Option 2 can also trigger safety along with your defensive activation. This difference is very subtle but important to parse out. Let's call them Safety Cueing Music Options 2A and 2B. Option 2A triggers safety alone. Option 2B triggers safety and the defensive state you're currently in. Compare this to State Alignment Music, which connects with your current dominant state. I'll use an example.
Example: Roger is stuck in shutdown.

ul: State Alignment Music: dark, moody, slow, bassy
Safety Cueing Music Option 1 as he is ready: faster, energetic, louder
Safety Cueing Music Option 2A music: lots of prosody
Safety Cueing Music Option 2B music: lots of prosody and slower, moody

blocks.p: The difference is subtle between State Alignment Music and Option 2B music. If Roger stays with State Alignment Music, nothing may change. He'll listen to the same songs on repeat ad nauseam, just like an angsty teen. Roger would need to attach mindfulness to the experience of his State Alignment Music to shift out of the defensive state. Option 2B also speaks to his shutdown but cues safety at the same time.

For example, loud heavy metal with screaming speaks to sympathetic activation, but an 80's rock power ballad speaks to sympathetic and safety since it contains so much prosody, especially in comparison to loud heavy metal with screaming. One more example: a somber song like Gary Jules' "Mad World" can speak to shutdown, while Bon Iver's "Blood Bank" speaks to shutdown and safety. "Blood Bank" contains a melancholic undertone and combines Bon Iver's warm vocal prosody. Give these two a listen, I bet you'll notice a distinct difference in their impact on you within the first 30 seconds. One feels more reinforcing of shutdown while the other feels like it's gently pulling the listener out of shutdown.

Be aware of how music affects your system. It doesn't matter so much if you can classify a song into State Alignment Music or Safety Cueing Music. Instead, focus on the general experience of how music affects your feelings of safety. Does a certain song help you feel more or less safe? How about a specific singer's voice? How about a genre?
As an aside, but important public service I must put forth, someone may read this (I'm sure it's not you) and wonder:
"Justin, how does country music help my system?"
The a priori and never-endingly true answer is country music doesn't help anyone ever and should be avoided at all costs in every context.

The words in music can influence your state and impact your rung on the Polyvagal ladder. Personal meaning combined with rhythm can be very effective in feeling a sense of safety or permitting defense. Song lyrics may provide you with further feelings of being understood, of connection, and emotional validity. The words could even trigger memories connected to safety or defense.

At the same time, the words could very well override the benefit of the music. Imagine listening to a song that helps you feel safe and gets you moving, then the singer launches into a tirade on something you find repulsive. The benefit of the music is lost due to the words. I doubt you listen to messages you find offensive or revolting, so we probably don't need to worry too much about this.

When it comes to safety cueing and anchoring, the feel of the music is more important than the words. The musicality of the instruments and vocal styles have the greatest effect on your autonomic nervous system neurocepting safety or danger from the music you listen to.

Similarly, if you use a low, monotone voice to tell a dog you love them, they will likely look down and away like they're in trouble. Same if you offer them a treat. You could probably tell your spouse, children, or friends you appreciate them without prosody, and they will look at you confused at the very least. (Especially if you do so with wide eyes.)

As you explore music, start by noticing what you feel drawn to or pushed away from. What feels safer than not? As you get better at recognizing how music affects you, create a Polyvagal playlist for safety songs. Then create more Polyvagal playlists that align with defensive activation. Use the safety playlist to cue safety passively or actively with movement for your safety practices. When you're ready to, use the defensively aligned playlists to permit defensive activation mindfully and assist with self-regulation.

blocks.why: Music is one sound anchor. This practice anchors through sound, at a pace that suits your state.

blocks.p: Turn on a random radio station or ask your smart device to play a random piece of music. As the music plays, allow yourself to feel it and observe your body's basic reactions, and answer these questions:

ul: Do you like or dislike it? Feel more or less grounded?
Does your body want to move?

blocks.p: Research musical types and sample them. Here are some starting points:

ul: Ben E. King, Etta James, Frank Sinatra
Yodeling, dombra, or other cultural music

ol: Music directly connects with neuroceptions of safety or danger.
Pay attention to how music affects you: what emotions and sensations arise?

Music can speak to your current state and help you experience it more fully. Additionally, it can assist in climbing your Polyvagal ladder by providing safety cues through prosody and other musical elements.

blocks.prompt: Did this provide you with any new experiences of safety?
Was this challenging for you? What about it was challenging?
Is this something you can continue to practice?
What music was the most helpful? Was there a specific genre, vocal style, or song?
